h1: The 7 Best Server Racks Under $700 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Server Racks Under $700: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 server racks under $700 compared on rack units, open frame versus enclosure, wheels and depth, from 6U to 18U.
summary: The AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels is the best all-round rack here: a steel frame, a standard 19-inch mount and casters that let you roll it out to reach the back. The NavePoint 18U Swing Gate is the pick when you need the most rack units and a lockable front. The RackPath 12U open frame is the budget-friendly, adjustable-depth choice for deeper gear.
intro: Rack buyers fixate on how many U they can get and forget the dimension that actually causes returns: depth. A 12U rack that looks perfect on paper cannot take a deep server or a tall power distribution unit if the posts only slide a short way. The second mistake is choosing a closed cabinet for a closet, where the heat has nowhere to go.

Every rack here sits well under the $700 limit, and six of the seven sit at $100 to $200, with one in the $200 to $500 bracket. We reviewed seven distinct models on rack unit height, open-frame versus enclosed design, adjustable depth and mobility. The scoring leaned toward steel construction, standard 19-inch mounting and ease of reaching the back panel.

products.name: AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels
products.verdict: A steel 12U rack on wheels that makes the back of your gear reachable.
products.description:
The AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels is a steel-framed rack with universal 19-inch rack-mount compatibility and a heavy-duty load rating. The casters are the feature that matters in practice: you can roll the rack away from a wall to swap cables, then roll it back.

It ranks first because it balances capacity and convenience better than the open frames below. Against the NavePoint 12U enclosure, it gives up the glass door, but the open design lets heat escape and your hands reach every port. Against the RIVECO 6U, it doubles the rack units.

Buy it for a home lab, a small office or a network closet with a floor you can roll across. The caveat is that the listing gives no exact load figure, so check the rating against your heaviest device.
cons: No door for dust or security
products.idealFor: Home labs and small offices that change cabling often.

products.name: NavePoint 18U Server Rack with Swing Gate
products.verdict: 18U of space behind a dual-hinged swing gate, with the most feature set here.
products.description:
The NavePoint 18U is a network rack with a dual-hinged front swing gate that opens like a door, giving you access to the equipment without pulling the unit off the wall. The 18U height is the tallest in this ranking, and the swing gate suits wall-mounted network installs.

It takes second place because it carries a higher price bracket of $200 to $500 against the $100 to $200 racks below, and only needs that extra height if your stack is genuinely large. Against the NavePoint 12U enclosure, it adds six rack units and a gate that makes cable work easier.

Choose it for a growing network with a patch panel, switches and a UPS. The caveat is cost and weight; it is the most expensive rack in this guide, and it does not roll.
cons: Needs a solid wall or floor spot
products.idealFor: Growing networks with several switches and a UPS.
products.skipIf: You have fewer than eight rack units of gear.

products.name: NavePoint 12U Server Rack Enclosure with Glass Door
products.verdict: A closed 12U cabinet with a glass door and removable side panels.
products.description:
The NavePoint 12U is an IT cabinet with a glass front door and removable side panels. Closing the equipment in keeps dust, pets and curious hands away, and the glass lets you read status lights without opening anything.

It ranks third because the enclosure is a different tool from the open frames above. You gain protection but lose airflow, so a heat-producing server in a cramped room needs ventilation planning. Against the 9U sibling, the 12U adds three units of space for little extra cost, so it is the better buy unless space is very tight.

Buy it for an office corner or a shared space where gear should look tidy. The caveat is that the listing gives few specifics, so confirm the load rating and the fan options before you commit.
products.idealFor: Shared offices where equipment should stay covered and neat.
products.skipIf: You run hot servers in a small room without ventilation.

products.name: RackPath 12U Open Frame Server Rack, Heavy Duty 4 Post Adjustable Depth
products.verdict: A 4-post open frame whose depth adjusts to fit longer servers.
products.description:
The RackPath 12U is a heavy-duty 4-post open frame with adjustable depth, listed at 29.3 inches high and 20.7 inches wide. Four posts mean equipment is supported at the front and back, which matters with a long server that would otherwise hang from the front rails.

It ranks fourth because it has no wheels, unlike the AxcessAbles 12U, and no door like the NavePoint enclosure. Its strength is depth adjustment, a feature fixed-depth 2-post racks do not have. Against the VEVOR 15U, it is shorter but gives clearer published dimensions.

Choose it if your servers or UPS are deep. The caveat is that the open frame has no security, so keep it in a closet or a lockable room.
products.idealFor: Home labs with deep servers or a rack UPS.
products.skipIf: You need a locking cabinet or a rolling rack.

products.name: VEVOR 15U Open Frame Server Rack
products.verdict: 15U of open frame with adjustable depth at the lower end of the price tier.
products.description:
The VEVOR 15U Open Frame Server Rack has adjustable depth and a strong load capacity, and it offers three more rack units than the 12U options for a price bracket of $100 to $200. That extra height is the reason to consider it.

It ranks fifth because the listing is vague: it names strong capacity and user-friendly design without publishing figures. Against the RackPath 12U, the VEVOR gives more height, while the RackPath lists real dimensions. Compared with the NavePoint 18U, it costs noticeably less but lacks the swing gate.

Buy it if you want the most rack units per dollar. The caveat is the missing detail, so check the load rating and depth range on the listing before you order.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want the most rack units for the least money.
products.skipIf: You want published load and dimension figures.

products.name: NavePoint 9U Server Rack Enclosure with Glass Door
products.verdict: The compact version of the glass-door cabinet, with removable side panels.
products.description:
The NavePoint 9U is the smaller sibling of the 12U cabinet, with the same glass door and removable side panels in a 9U IT cabinet. It fits under a desk or in a corner where a taller rack would not.

It ranks sixth because three fewer units is a real limit: once you add a switch, a patch panel, a router and a UPS, 9U fills quickly. Against the 12U version, the saving is small, so the 9U only makes sense when height is the constraint rather than money.

Buy it for a small business or home network with a short stack. The caveat is the closed design, which retains heat, so avoid putting a hot server inside without airflow.
products.idealFor: Short network stacks where height is limited.
products.skipIf: You expect to add more equipment next year.

products.name: RIVECO 6U Open Frame Server Rack with Wheels, Heavy Duty 4 Post
products.verdict: A 6U, 4-post cold-rolled steel frame on wheels for the smallest setups.
products.description:
The RIVECO 6U is a 4-post open frame in SPCC cold-rolled steel, 19.7 inches (500 mm) wide and 21.7 inches deep, with wheels and quick assembly. It is the smallest rack here and the only 6U option.

It ranks last because six units is a real ceiling: a switch, a patch panel and a small UPS fill it. It is freestanding and mobile, and its published dimensions are more specific than most. Against the AxcessAbles 12U, you give up half the space.

Choose it for a compact home network or an audio-video corner. The caveat is the limited depth of 21.7 inches, which excludes many full-depth servers.
products.idealFor: Compact home networks and small AV corners.
products.skipIf: You own deep rack servers or plan to expand.

methodology.title: Rack units and layout
methodology.description: We scored whether the U height matches realistic gear stacks, from a small switch to a growing home lab.

methodology.title: Frame versus enclosure
methodology.description: Open frames earn credit for airflow and access, enclosures for dust protection and a tidy look.

methodology.title: Depth and dimensions
methodology.description: Adjustable depth and published measurements decide whether a rack will accept deeper servers and UPS units.

methodology.title: Build and mobility
methodology.description: Steel construction, 4-post design and wheels affect how sturdy the rack is and how easily you can reach cables.

methodology.title: Listing transparency
methodology.description: Racks that publish load ratings and sizes score higher than those that rely on vague wording.

whatMatters.detail: One U is 1.75 inches of vertical mounting space, and every device is measured in it. A 12U rack holds twelve of those. Add up your gear, including patch panels and a UPS, then leave a few spare units for growth. On a listing, check the usable U, not the outside height.

Open frames let heat escape and give instant access to cables, but offer no dust or security protection. Enclosures such as the NavePoint 12U keep gear covered, though they trap heat. Pick open frames for a closet and enclosures for a visible office corner, and look for vent or fan provisions.

Servers vary widely in depth, and a rack that is too shallow cannot close around them. The RackPath 12U and VEVOR 15U advertise adjustable depth, while the RIVECO 6U lists 21.7 inches fixed. Measure your deepest device and check the listing's depth range before buying.

A 4-post rack supports equipment at the front and rear, which is safer for heavy or long devices than a 2-post design that holds only the front. The RackPath, RIVECO and VEVOR are open-frame racks of this type. Look for the post count in the title, and be cautious when it is missing.

Casters let you roll the rack out to reach the back, which is a huge help for rewiring. The AxcessAbles 12U and RIVECO 6U include them. Wheels add height and can lower stability, so look for lockable casters, and confirm the rating covers a fully loaded rack.

faq.q: Will standard network gear fit these racks?
faq.a: Yes, if it is 19-inch rack-mountable. The AxcessAbles 12U lists universal 19-inch compatibility, and the other racks follow the same standard. Always check depth first, since the RIVECO 6U allows only 21.7 inches.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with server racks?
faq.a: Buying by height and ignoring depth. A 12U RackPath adjusts depth to fit long servers, while a fixed-depth frame may not close around them. Measure your deepest device before choosing.

faq.q: Is the NavePoint 18U worth it over the VEVOR 15U?
faq.a: Only if you need the extra three units and the swing gate. The NavePoint 18U sits in the $200 to $500 bracket, while the VEVOR 15U stays at $100 to $200. For most home labs, the VEVOR is enough.

faq.q: How do I set up a rack safely?
faq.a: Put the heaviest gear low, level the rack and lock the casters if it has them. On the AxcessAbles 12U or RIVECO 6U, engage the wheel locks before loading. Leave space for cables and airflow.

faq.q: How should I handle heat in an enclosure?
faq.a: Leave gaps between devices, use blanking panels and consider a fan. The NavePoint 9U and 12U close in the equipment, so ventilation matters more than with open frames like the RackPath.

faq.q: Can a rack sit on carpet?
faq.a: It can, but wheeled racks like the AxcessAbles 12U roll poorly on thick carpet and may tip when loaded. Use a hard surface or lock the casters, and keep heavy gear low.

finalTake: The AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels is the best all-round rack under $700, because steel, a standard mount and casters cover most needs. Choose the NavePoint 18U if you need height and a swing gate, and the RackPath 12U for deep gear. Go for an enclosed NavePoint only when dust or looks matter, and the RIVECO 6U for very small setups.
